top_level_objectives: Explain the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion of outer planets.
Differentiate between geocentric and heliocentric explanations for retrograde motion.
Relate relative orbital speeds to the observed retrograde effect.
Compare the retrograde motion of different outer planets.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as observed from Earth.
key_visuals: A simulated night sky showing the constellations.
A representation of Mars moving eastward against the background stars.
Mars then slowing, reversing to westward motion (retrograde loop).
Mars resuming its eastward motion.
student_actions: Observe Mars's apparent motion over an extended period (simulated).
Identify the start and end of Mars's retrograde loop.
Describe the observed path of Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: To illustrate the complexity of explaining retrograde motion with a geocentric model.
key_visuals: An Earth-centered solar system model.
Mars's orbit around Earth with epicycles to explain retrograde motion.
The Sun and other planets also orbiting Earth.
student_actions: Manipulate the epicycle and deferent for Mars.
Attempt to match the observed retrograde loop using epicycles.
Reflect on the complexity of this model.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the heliocentric model and provide an overhead view of planetary orbits.
key_visuals: A Sun-centered solar system model.
Concentric circular or elliptical orbits for Earth and Mars.
The Sun at the center.
Indications of orbital speeds for Earth and Mars.
student_actions: Observe the relative positions and orbital speeds of Earth and Mars.
Identify the Sun as the central body.
Compare the smoothness of orbits to the geocentric model.

scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate how Earth's faster orbit causes the apparent retrograde motion of Mars.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model with Earth and Mars in motion.
An indicator showing when Earth is passing Mars.
A viewpoint shift to simulate the 'Earthbound view' during the overtake.
The resulting retrograde loop appearing in the 'Earthbound view' during the overtake.
student_actions: Play the animation of Earth and Mars orbits.
Note the period when Earth overtakes Mars.
Correlate the overtake period with the appearance of retrograde motion from Earth's perspective.

scenes.brief_purpose: To reinforce the concept of relative motion causing apparent backward movement using a familiar analogy.
key_visuals: A visual of two cars on a highway.
One car (Earth) overtaking a slower car (Mars).
A simulated view from inside the faster car, showing the slower car appearing to move backward.
Labels indicating relative speed and overtaking.
student_actions: Relate the car scenario to the Earth-Mars orbital motion.
Explain why the slower car appears to move backward.

scenes.brief_purpose: To compare the retrograde motion of Mars with that of Jupiter and Saturn.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model showing Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Simulated retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Visual cues indicating the duration and magnitude of each planet's retrograde loop.
Orbital paths and distances from the Sun.
student_actions: Observe the retrograde loops of Jupiter and Saturn.
Compare the duration and apparent size of the loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain how distance from the Sun affects the prominence of retrograde motion.
